measurement.whatV2Said: v2's dependencyGraph read 'This artifact defines the graph's required members, not the populated per-OS table.' That was accurate and appropriately modest. v3 upgrades it to 'defines members AND the assignment rules' and adds the unqualified determinism sentence. The overclaim is introduced by the edit under review, not inherited.
measurement.counterexample1_LTCB: layerTaxonomy's own L-TCB entry reads 'platform base/host-ABI TCB declared by the signed closure; identity rules are DR-126's', and ID-DEP-K2 — unchanged in v3 — reads 'L-TCB identity rules are that row's.' Whether a given platform library is L-DIST or L-TCB is therefore decided by DR-126, not by these rules. The artifact says so twice and then says it owns the assignment rules.
measurement.counterexample2_LDISTvsLHOST: For any node that is NOT the shared executable, nothing in graphRules assigns L-DIST versus L-HOST. layerAssignmentCardinality governs how many layers and which combinations, never which layer. A library linked by both surfaces is assignable either way, and two conforming inventories would differ.
measurement.counterexample3_LEVAL: layerAssignmentCardinality makes L-EVAL exclusive, and sharedExecutableRepresentation fixes the shared node at exactly {L-DIST, L-HOST} — yet that same rule invokes L-EVAL in its closing clause, 'does not move ... effects into L-EVAL'. If the pure evaluation core is compiled into the shared binary, which is the ordinary shape of a single-executable native design, no node can carry L-EVAL. The rules do not say whether the eval core must then be separately published or simply goes unrepresented.
measurement.soTheClaimIsFalse: 'Deterministic' is refuted by three foreseeable cases, one of which the artifact contradicts two keys away in the same object.

shouldFix.whyShouldFixAndNotBlocker: Nothing is orphaned and no ownership is exported — ID-DEP-K2 still correctly holds the L-TCB identity rules at DR-126, so unlike the v1 blocker this does not leave an obligation unowned between rows. The SATISFIED path is untouched. And the repair's actual target genuinely is deterministic: the shared executable has exactly one lawful representation. This is an overstated summary, not a broken rule.
shouldFix.whyItIsNotMerelyAdvisory: It sits on the two rostered paths this successor exists to change, so it is the new content rather than inherited noise. It is the kind of sentence a later successor quotes to argue DR-101's layering fragment is fully discharged, and 'defines ... the assignment rules' with the definite article reads as completeness. A row whose contract claims to have made layer assignment deterministic is a row that looks closer to closure than it is — and OBL-D-LAY points the layering obligation straight at this object.
shouldFix.minimumRepair: Scope both sentences to what the rules do. For example: these rules fix layer-set cardinality, lawful overlap and the shared-executable representation; which layer a non-shared node takes follows layerTaxonomy, and the L-TCB boundary is DR-126's per ID-DEP-K2. Restoring v2's 'required members' framing in dependencyGraph, with the graphRules pointer added, would also do it. Separately, one clause saying whether L-EVAL is expected to be a separately published file would close counterexample 3.

advisories.title: Roster hygiene: /date is rostered but did not change, and the universal closure sentence was dropped
advisories.detail: Two things. First, the roster names /date and even emphasises it ('/date is on this roster'), but v2 and v3 are both dated 2026-08-15 — it is the one rostered path that did not move, where v2's roster had no padding at all. Second, v2's method carried the falsifiable universal 'Every path neither the roster nor succession metadata names is unchanged from v1.' v3 keeps the label 'Closed roster' but drops that sentence.
advisories.whyOnlyAdvisory: Neither costs anything here. An over-inclusive roster cannot falsify a closure claim, only weaken its precision. And I tested the closure claim on its merits — 15 changed paths, all rostered — so the dropped sentence would have held had it been made. The /date emphasis is also defensible as a standing reminder for future successors even in a round where the date happens not to move.
advisories.suggestedFix: Restore v2's universal sentence; it is what makes the roster testable rather than merely asserted.

advisories.title: nodeIdentity's escape hatch names an edge kind the artifact never defines
advisories.subjectQuote: Duplicate path or duplicate sha256-under-different-path is a failed successor unless the second is an explicit alias edge, which this artifact does not mint.
advisories.detail: edgeRelation defines one relation, directed 'requires' from consumer to dependency. An 'alias edge' appears nowhere else in the artifact and, by the clause's own admission, is not minted here. So the exception is inert but names a mechanism a successor could claim without any definition to conform to.
advisories.whyOnlyAdvisory: It cannot reopen the repair. The shared executable is protected by a separate unconditional prohibition in sharedExecutableRepresentation — 'Do not emit two nodes with the same sha256' — with no alias exception attached, and the specific rule governs. I checked this specifically because an inert exception next to a duplicate-node rule is exactly where a repair like this would leak.
advisories.suggestedFix: Either define the alias edge in edgeRelation or drop the exception and let the duplicate rule stand unconditional.

verdictStatement: The repair works. I attacked the shared executable every way the dispatch names — L-DIST-only, L-HOST-only, duplicated, exclusively assigned — and every one is explicitly shut, with the {L-DIST, L-HOST} overlap confined to that single node so it cannot spread. Node granularity, roots, edge direction and layer-set cardinality are all defined, authority non-migration survives the merge, and nothing from the v1 or v2 repairs unwound under the new edit. The closed roster holds: 15 changed paths, all rostered, and the two paths declared historical are byte-identical rather than quietly amended. What fails is the sentence written around the repair. v3 upgraded dependencyGraph from v2's modest 'defines the graph's required members' to 'defines members AND the assignment rules', and added 'These rules make assignment deterministic.' Neither holds. The rules fix cardinality, lawful overlap and the shared-executable representation; they never say which layer a non-shared node takes. The L-DIST versus L-TCB boundary is decided by DR-126 — the artifact says so twice, at layerTaxonomy's L-TCB entry and at ID-DEP-K2, which v3 left unchanged while claiming to own the assignment rules. And L-EVAL is unassignable for a shared binary containing the pure evaluation core, in the same rule that invokes L-EVAL. Both sentences sit on rostered paths this successor exists to change, so this is new content, not inherited noise, and OBL-D-LAY points the layering obligation straight at the object that now overstates itself. One clause of scoping fixes it.

coordinatorNote: REJECT of the artifact, not a disposition of the row. DR-101 stays OPEN at file 08 line 283. I accepted v2 and reject v3, so the direction of travel should be clear: this is not a regression and not a reopening of anything settled. The CODEX-V2-S1 repair is sound and should carry into a v4 unchanged — my single finding is one overstated summary sentence on two rostered paths, repairable without touching a rule. Three things to weigh. First, the fix is genuinely small: scope 'deterministic' to what the rules do and restore v2's framing in dependencyGraph; a v4 that changes only those two strings would, on my measurement, carry zero blockers and zero SHOULD-FIX. Second, I was instructed not to open the Codex v2 verdict, so v3's record of it at /appliesFindingsOf/codexv2 is digest-matched but content-unverified by me — if the coordinator needs that record confirmed, it needs the Codex lane or a reviewer without my restriction. Third, my four v2 advisories remain openly unfolded by v3's own declaration, which I verified item by item; they are the coordinator's to accept or carry, and none of them blocks anything.
